notes.shape: The yield curve represents the relationship between Treasury yields across maturities, from 1 month to 30 years, with an upward slope indicating higher yields on longer-term bonds reflecting positive growth expectations. Historically, an inverted curve—where short-term yields exceed long-term yields—has preceded US recessions by 6 to 18 months. As of now, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.71% with the 10Y-2Y spread at 0.36 percentage points, showing a positively sloped curve. This contrasts with 2022-2024 when the curve was inverted, having spent significant time below 0.0 points, the deepest inversion threshold in the available series.
notes.signal: The 10-year minus 2-year (2s10s) spread is a widely used recession indicator, with inversion (spread below zero) signaling economic downturn risk. The curve was inverted from 2022 through 2024 but has since re-steepened above zero to 0.36 points, reducing immediate recession concerns. However, the New York Fed’s recession probability remains elevated at 31%, reflecting lingering economic risks not fully resolved by the yield curve normalization. It is important to acknowledge that the yield curve often un-inverts before recessions actually commence, limiting the spread's predictive precision in timing.
notes.now: Currently, the yield curve has transitioned to a normal upward slope, and the 2s10s spread’s return to positive territory suggests diminished recession threat compared to the prior inversion period. Nonetheless, the NY Fed’s moderate 31% recession probability indicates ongoing economic caution, warranting close monitoring without definitive conclusions on recession timing.
